tagline: Four river systems link forest roads, a mill bridge and power-company country.
intro: The West Cascades Scenic Byway follows four river systems through forest on the western side of Oregon’s Cascades. Near Westfir, the road twists along the North Fork of the Middle Fork Willamette through a canyon with thousand-foot rock walls. Oregon’s transportation department describes the drive through its old-growth forests, lakes and snowcapped volcanic peaks, allowing seven to nine hours for the 220-mile route. It is a National Scenic Byway. The Clackamas section hugs the river, with riffles, rapids and pools beside the road; on the North Santiam, the descent flattens as it reaches Detroit.

The roads brought work as well as travelers. In 1932, Scott Young bought property at Marion Forks, where his family built cabins and a cookhouse to serve crews working on Highways 20 and 22. At Westfir, the lumber company built Office Bridge in 1944 to carry trucks to its mill and mill pond. The southern forest-road section bears the name Aufderheide, honoring a forester.

Drive north from Westfir past Cougar Reservoir to the McKenzie River, then follow OR 126 toward Santiam Junction. OR 22 follows the North Santiam downhill toward Detroit Lake. At Detroit, Forest Road 46 follows the Breitenbush River toward Ripplebrook. There, join OR 224 beside the Clackamas and continue to Estacada.

moments.title: Office Bridge
moments.text: Office Bridge carried logging and lumber trucks to the Westfir Lumber Company’s mill, with a separate walkway for pedestrians. The span crosses the North Fork Middle Fork Willamette River at Westfir. Built in 1944, it replaced a bridge from 1941 that had washed away. The company’s offices stood across the river from the mill. At 180 feet, it is Oregon’s longest covered bridge. Its triple Howe truss carried the industrial traffic. After the mill burned, Lane County acquired the bridge through tax foreclosure in 1992. Structural work stabilized it the following year, and its roof was replaced in 2002.
moments.notice: The covered bridge has a separate pedestrian walkway.

moments.title: Breitenbush
moments.text: Breitenbush’s name records a surveyor’s mistaken recollection. In 1874, Oregon legislator John Minto led a party looking for a pass over the central Cascades. They encountered a hunter whom Minto remembered as John Breitenbush; people in the Lower Santiam knew him as Lewis Breitenbucher. The map name became accepted by the end of the nineteenth century. Hot springs later drew visitors along improved trails, roads and bridges. By 1901, a horse pack train from Detroit served the springs. The community’s post office operated from 1928 to 1953, during its development as a hot springs resort.

moments.title: Three Lynx
moments.text: Three Lynx began as Camp 8, a construction settlement built by the Portland Railway, Light and Power Company as early as 1923. Its first seven cabins, mostly made by the Aladdin Company, became the beginnings of a permanent worker community. Powerhouse modernization reduced the number of workers needed locally, contributing to depopulation. The school closed in 1988 and was demolished in 2014. In 2018, the company began looking for a successor to take responsibility for the town. The final permanent residents left in January 2020; the Riverside Fire destroyed most houses that September. The remaining houses were subsequently demolished.

practical: Office Bridge: Forest Roads 19 and 46 are generally closed by snowfall from November 15 to April 30. (checked 2026-10-11)
